steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?. This part covers Try it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Sometimes two pieces are loose at once, and you can take only one now. A good default is to take the **higher-value** piece first, then see whether the other can run. [I] That default comes from these two boards, not from a law. Both orders are shown, so you can compare. Two boards after them show when the order matters less.

steps.caption: Two loose pieces: the rook on b8, attacked by the bishop, and the knight on d4, attacked by the rook.

line.say: The bishop takes the bigger prize, the rook. The knight is still attacked.
Black rescues the knight, but the rook is gone for good.

claims.statement: Both the rook and the knight are loose.
Taking the rook first is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: The other order: the rook takes the knight first.

line.say: The rook takes the knight first. Now the black rook on b8 is still attacked.
The black rook runs. White won only the knight.

claims.statement: Taking the knight first wins only the knight.
It is worse than taking the rook first.

steps.text: The default bends when the smaller piece cannot run. A knight **pinned** to its king cannot move, so both orders win both pieces. [I] The reverse case: if the bigger piece cannot run but the smaller one can, take the smaller one first, before it escapes. Always ask which piece can actually get away.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 is pinned to its king by the rook, so it cannot run. Take the bigger prize first.

line.say: The king leaves the file, but it is White's move: the knight is taken before it can run.
The rook takes the knight. Both pieces are won.

claims.statement: Both the knight and the rook are loose.
Either capture is among the engine's best moves.

steps.caption: The other order also works: the rook takes the pinned knight with check, so the king must answer and cannot guard the rook.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and gives check.
The king steps out of check.
The bishop takes the rook. Both pieces are won.

claims.statement: Both the knight and the rook are loose.
Either capture is among the engine's best moves.

steps.text: Your own pieces can be loose too. After **every** move your opponent makes, check two lists: their loose pieces and yours. [H] My guess is that players miss their own loose pieces more than the enemy's, because after your own move your mind is on your plan. [I] An unchecked scan fails most often on your own side. I have not measured either.

steps.caption: Both lists on one board. Their loose piece: the bishop on g4, attacked by the h3 pawn. Yours: the rook on d1, attacked by that bishop.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 is loose.
The rook on d1 is loose.

steps.caption: Best answer: take the attacker. One capture wins their piece and ends the danger to yours.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop. Nothing attacks the rook on d1 any more.

claims.statement: The pawn wins the bishop.
No white piece is loose afterwards.

steps.caption: Now you cannot capture the bishop. Black has just moved it to g4, attacking your undefended rook. Fix one: move the piece away.

line.say: The rook steps to a square the bishop does not attack.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 is loose.
No white piece is loose after the rook moves.

steps.caption: Fix two: block the line. A piece between the bishop and the rook stops the attack.

line.say: The pawn blocks the bishop's line. The bishop now attacks the pawn, and the g2 pawn guards it.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose after the block.
The pawn on g2 defends f3.

steps.caption: The answer to the last task, as a fix. The bishop on c4 is attacked and undefended, so it must move.

line.say: The bishop retreats to a square the knight on d6 does not attack.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is loose.
No white piece is loose after the retreat.

steps.caption: Fix three: defend the piece. A pawn on b3 guards the bishop, so a knight capture would be answered by a recapture.

line.say: The pawn guards the bishop on c4.
...the pawn takes back: bishop for knight, an even trade.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is loose before the move.
No white piece is loose after the defence.

steps.text: Your answers to an attacked piece: **capture** the attacker, **move** away, **block** the line, **defend** the piece, or **counterattack** with a bigger threat. Defending works well when the attacker is worth as much as your piece or more. A cheaper attacker, such as a bishop against a rook, still wins value even against a defended piece. A counterattack must really be bigger.
